prompt: In which quadrant does an angle of $-400^\circ$ in standard position terminate?
hint: First find a positive coterminal angle by adding full turns of $360^\circ$ — the minus sign matters the whole way.

hints.text: First find a positive coterminal angle by adding full turns of $360^\circ$ — the minus sign matters the whole way.

hints.title: 🪜 Try a simpler one
hints.text: Warm up with $-30^\circ$: adding one turn gives $-30 + 360 = 330^\circ$, just below the positive $x$-axis in Quadrant IV. Add turns the same way here, but you will need two of them.
$-40 + 360 = 320^\circ$, and $270^\circ < 320^\circ < 360^\circ$, so it lands in Quadrant IV.

explanation: Add full turns until the angle is positive: $-400 + 360 = -40$, then $-40 + 360 = 320$.
Since $320^\circ$ falls between $270^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, the terminal side is in Quadrant IV.

alternativeExplanations.title: Spin it clockwise
steps: Turning $-360^\circ$ is one full clockwise lap that puts you back at the start.
That leaves $40^\circ$ more of clockwise turn, which dips just below the positive $x$-axis.
Just below the positive $x$-axis is Quadrant IV.

alternativeExplanations.title: ⚠️ The trap here
steps: The trap answer is Quadrant I — dropping the minus sign, reducing $400^\circ$ to $40^\circ$, and stopping there. But $-400^\circ$ turns the other way, so it cannot land where $+40^\circ$ does.
Handle the sign first: for a negative angle, ADD $360^\circ$ (as many times as needed) instead of subtracting. That gives $320^\circ$, and Quadrant IV.
